title: Sibbach v. Wilson & Co. (1941)
summary: The Federal Rule authorizing a physical examination fell within the rulemaking authority Congress conferred.
notes:
The assigned discussion concerns the Rule’s validity; it does not supply every aspect of the original discovery and contempt proceedings.

Sibbach was injured in Indiana and sued in federal court in Illinois, whose law did not allow court-ordered physical examinations; ordered to submit under Rule 35, she refused and was held in contempt under Rule 37, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed.

Although it upheld Rule 35, the Court (Justice Roberts, 5-4) actually reversed the contempt judgment because Rule 37 as then written did not authorize contempt for refusing a physical examination; Justice Frankfurter's dissent was joined by Justices Black, Douglas and Murphy. The majority's test, whether a rule 'really regulates procedure', is the language the Shady Grove plurality later adopted.

sections.Parties: Sibbach, a litigant whose physical condition was at issue, challenged an order for a medical examination under the Federal Rules.
sections.Material Facts: The disputed federal procedure permitted a physical examination that the plaintiff argued could not be imposed under the relevant state approach. The objection emphasized the importance of personal bodily interests and whether the Rule exceeded delegated authority.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court upheld the Rule’s validity. The casebook discusses that holding through Hanna and the later Rules Enabling Act debate.
sections.Issue: Did the examination Rule regulate judicial procedure within Congress’s delegation, or did its intrusion into an important personal interest invalidate it?
sections.Holding: The Rule was valid as a regulation of procedure.
sections.Reasoning: The majority asked whether the Rule really regulated the judicial process for enforcing rights. The importance of the affected interest did not by itself remove the matter from procedural rulemaking authority. Later opinions debate how this test interacts with the Act’s separate prohibition on abridging, enlarging, or modifying substantive rights.

learning.why: The Federal Rule authorizing a physical examination fell within the rulemaking authority Congress conferred.

topics.cp-rules-enabling: The Court upheld the examination rule as regulating procedure under the Enabling Act.
topics.cp-erie: An important personal interest is not automatically a substantive right in the precise Enabling Act sense.
topics.cp-usc-2072: Sibbach is the first Supreme Court reading of the Rules Enabling Act's procedure/substantive-right line and supplies the 'really regulates procedure' test.
topics.cp-rule-scope: The Court also read Rule 37 narrowly, holding it did not authorize contempt, which is a rule-scope question distinct from validity.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Frankfurter’s dissent emphasized the invasion of the person and questioned whether congressional inaction on the Rules could establish affirmative approval of so significant a change.
